---
title: Tabsets
---

Tabsets present alternative versions of content — for example, the same
instructions for different languages or operating systems — as clickable
tabs, with one tab's content visible at a time.

## Creating a tabset

Wrap the content in a div with the `panel-tabset` class. Each top-level
heading inside the div becomes a tab; the content that follows it, up to
the next heading of the same level, becomes that tab's pane:

````markdown
::: {.panel-tabset}

## R

```r
fizz_buzz <- function(fbnums = 1:50) {
  output <- dplyr::case_when(
    fbnums %% 15 == 0 ~ "FizzBuzz",
    fbnums %% 3 == 0 ~ "Fizz",
    fbnums %% 5 == 0 ~ "Buzz",
    TRUE ~ as.character(fbnums)
  )
  print(output)
}
```

## Python

```python
def fizz_buzz(num):
  if num % 15 == 0:
    print("FizzBuzz")
  elif num % 5 == 0:
    print("Buzz")
  elif num % 3 == 0:
    print("Fizz")
  else:
    print(num)
```

:::
````

This renders as:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## R

```r
fizz_buzz(1:15)
```

## Python

```python
fizz_buzz(15)
```

:::

The first tab is selected by default. To pre-select a different tab, add
the `active` class to its heading:

```markdown
## Python {.active}
```

No heading inside a tabset appears in the page's table of contents —
neither the headings that define the tabs nor any deeper headings you
write inside a tab body. Only regular section headings are listed.

This keeps the table of contents usable. Tabs very often share the same
sub-headings — one per provider, language, or platform — so listing them
would fill the contents with repeated entries that give the reader no way
to tell them apart, and every entry but the one in the open tab would
point at hidden content. Headings inside a tab still work normally in
every other respect: they render, they get an id, and you can link to
them directly.

## Tab groups

Tabsets can be linked so that selecting a tab in one switches every other
tabset in the same group. Give each tabset a `group` attribute:

```markdown
::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
```

When a reader picks a tab (say, **Python**), every `group="language"`
tabset on the page with a matching tab name follows, and the choice is
remembered in the browser — pages visited later start with the same tab
selected. This is ideal for documentation that offers parallel
instructions per language, operating system, or framework.

Tabsets are supported in HTML formats with a Bootstrap theme. In other
formats the tab headings render as ordinary stacked sections.
